title: docs: generate the ipc api reference from the contracts
body:
## Why

`docs/API.md` was 1,095 hand-written lines, and a third of it was wrong.

It documented **three namespaces that do not exist** — `agent`, `search`, `shortcuts` — the `agent` section alone running ~76 lines of methods and events for a namespace with no contract. It **omitted nine real ones**. And its header read *Last updated: 2026-08-17*, which made it worse: the date told readers it was current.

The fiction went deeper than the missing namespaces. `credentials` was documented with four methods when the real contract has one. `dialog` with three, real answer one. `jobs` with nine, real answer five. `documents.import` and `ai.setProviderKey` had the wrong signatures entirely. An event, `ai:pull-progress`, appears nowhere in the repo — pull progress actually rides `job.stream` on the generic job channel.

## What changed

`scripts/gen-api-docs.mjs` emits the whole page from `packages/shared/src/ipc/contracts/`, wired as `gen:api` / `gen:api:check` alongside the three generators that already exist, and gated in CI's `lint-format` job.

Two design choices worth calling out:

**Signatures are copied verbatim from source text**, never re-rendered from a parsed type. Nothing can come out plausibly-wrong, which is the failure this page existed to demonstrate. Multi-line params and their inline field docs survive intact.

**It fails loudly rather than guessing.** An unsupported member kind, a non-literal channel entry, a missing interface — all exit 1 with a message saying to extend the generator. Proven by mutation: adding an index signature produces `unsupported contract member kind IndexSignature … extend the generator rather than guessing at its shape`.

## Prose was migrated, not deleted

The old page held real knowledge no signature carries — that `temperature` overrides `intent` on every adapter, that `embed`'s `model` field is on the wire but ignored, that `save` merge-upserts on `jobUrl`. Thirteen such facts moved into TSDoc on the owning contract method, each re-verified against the implementation first rather than copied on faith.

Deliberately dropped: the three fictional namespaces, and a hand-maintained 23-item board list that had already drifted — it was missing `jobicy` **while sitting next to a pointer at the canonical constant**. The pointer stayed.

107 of 174 methods now carry TSDoc. The other 67 render as signature-only entries. That is honest: the gaps are visible where a developer can fix them, instead of covered by prose that may or may not still be true.

## The gate provably fails

Adding a method to a contract and running `gen:api:check`:

```
Generated docs/API.md — 31 namespaces, 175 methods, 108 with TSDoc (67 without).
 | [`geocode`](#geocode) | 1 → 2
+#### `geocode.gateMutationProbe`
[ELIFECYCLE] Command failed with exit code 1.
```

Reverted, exit 0. Verified twice, independently.

Also worth recording: the generator's first version rendered an empty `*_CHANNELS` as "this namespace exposes no invoke channels" — **false** for `notifications`, which has nine live commands invoking their Tauri names directly. That is exactly the plausible-but-wrong statement this work exists to eliminate, so the last commit replaces the inference with the structural fact.

## Verification

`pnpm test` 7,136 passed · `pnpm typecheck` 13/13 · `pnpm lint:strict --max-warnings 0` clean · `prettier --check docs/API.md` clean (the generator formats its own output through prettier's API, so the check can never fight the formatter) · `check:adr-citations` · `check:agent-system`.

`AGENTS.md` rule 14 now sends a new capability to `pnpm gen:api` and says prose belongs in contract TSDoc, so the next person doesn't hand-edit a generated file and lose it.

* **Documentation**
  * Expanded IPC API documentation with clearer behavior, limitations, privacy requirements, scoring options, data handling, and integration details.
  * API documentation is now generated consistently from documented contracts, reducing manual maintenance and improving accuracy.

* **Chores**
  * Added commands to generate API documentation and check for outdated generated content.
  * Continuous integration now detects documentation drift and reports required updates.

title: fix: make in-flight backend work survive navigation, and stop logs leaking paths
body:
## What this is

An audit of the nine route-scoped entries in `check-event-subscriptions.mjs` found **eight of the nine notes were wrong**. Fixing them turned up six real defects behind them, so this PR carries both: the corrections, the fixes, and two guards so neither class rots again.

## The notes were wrong, and nothing could tell us

Three notes described a loss that had already been fixed, four understated it, one named a cause the code does not have. Only the activity-feed note was accurate.

They rot because nothing coupled them to the code: #1019 fixed the jobs scrape and never touched the note beside it, and #1025 later edited that very file without noticing the note next to it was by then obsolete. The guard enforced that a note **exists**, never that it is **true**.

Each route-scoped entry now carries a content hash of the file it describes, and the check fails when the file drifts, printing the note so re-reading costs seconds. It fired on this PR's own merge for four files — that is the mechanism working.

**Known blind spot, recorded in the file:** the hash covers the declared file only, so a note also goes stale when behaviour changes in something that file merely *calls*. Both misses came from this batch — `JobsPage`'s defect was fixed inside `useScraping.ts`, `update-section`'s inside the updater service — and neither declared file was touched. Hashing the import graph would fire on nearly every commit and be ignored within a week, so those two entries say in their own text that they were fixed elsewhere.

## The six defects

**You get invited to start expensive work that is already running.** Returning to Settings mid-update rendered a live "Check now"; clicking it cleared `downloaded_bytes`, discarding a finished download and forcing a full re-fetch, with no re-entry guard. Returning to onboarding mid-pull re-showed Download; clicking it started a *second* multi-GB pull, because `ai_pull_model` used `job_start` rather than the `job_start_exclusive` that already existed.

**The failure reason never arrived.** A résumé run that failed while you were on another tab left no error at all — you came back to the plain wizard as if you had never pressed Generate, because `error` was only ever written by the live listener. Autopilot had the same shape, plus a `staleTime` hole that showed an idle card with an enabled Run button for a live run.

**Jobs lied about progress.** The default board set is one board, so `scrape:progress` fires once, at the end — after a remount the bar asserted a false 0% for the rest of the run, while the tracker already held the true fraction and the watchdog fetched it and threw it away. A scrape that *failed* off-page came back with no explanation at all.

## Path leaks in logs

145 `log::…("{e}")` sites audited against rule 1 of `AGENTS.md`. **100 fixed**, the rest traced and declared safe with a reason. Not a blanket replacement — 33 of the scraping sites turned out genuinely safe because `scraping::http::fetch_text` already calls `.without_url()`, and replacing them would have discarded useful diagnostics to fix nothing.

The one worth naming: `linkedin/api_client/mod.rs` bypasses that chokepoint with a raw `client.get(url).send()`, so a transport failure logged the full guest-search URL **including the user's free-text keywords and location**.

`scripts/check-log-error-leaks.mjs` now fails in both directions — an undeclared leak, and a declared entry that no longer matches.

## Verification

- `cargo test --all-features --locked` — 4,349 passed
- `pnpm test` — 7,102 passed · `pnpm typecheck` · `pnpm lint:strict --max-warnings 0` — clean
- both new guards plus `check:agent-system` green

Every fix was mutation-checked by execution, not by reasoning: the guard removed, the test watched go red, the guard restored.

Two things I checked rather than assumed. Two Rust tests failed once under full parallelism and passed on a clean re-run; neither file is in this diff, so they are pre-existing flakes, confirmed by re-running rather than by asserting it. And a new leak test dialled the discard port, which Windows leaves hanging until its own timeout — over a minute on every run, now bounded to 0.52s.

## Note for review

`extension_bridge/mod.rs` crossed the R8 LOC cap once its fixes landed, so its token/opt-in persistence split into `persist.rs`, following that file's own existing `autotrack.rs` precedent.

title: fix(scraping): wire the freehire params their spec never documented
body:
Acts on issue #1026, where the freehire maintainer disclosed that our PR #1008
"Known limits" section had found three defects in **their** published spec —
`openapi.yaml` documented 17 of ~35 real query parameters.

## The actual bug

`freehire.rs` took `_date_filter: Option<&str>` — underscore-prefixed, accepted
and thrown away, because the documented spec had no date parameter. It has one:
`posted_within_days`. Our date filter had nowhere to go and silently did
nothing.

## Verified against the live API, not taken on trust

Every claim in the issue was checked by hitting `/api/v1/agent/jobs/search`
directly and re-reading the live `openapi.yaml`:

| Claim | Result |
|---|---|
| `posted_within_days` exists | ✅ integer days, `minimum: 1`; `=1` cut 1,477,440 → 66,802 |
| `reality=fresh` exists | ✅ cut the catalogue to 662,112 (~45%) |
| `meta.ignored_params` shape | ✅ a `country=gb` typo returns **200** + the **full unfiltered set**, with `did_you_mean: "countries"`. A clean request omits the key entirely — not an empty array |
| `X-RateLimit-*` on success | ✅ `300/299/1` on the agent endpoint |

**Not** independently verified: the 600/300 req/min ceilings and the leaky-bucket
behaviour under sustained load. Load-testing someone else's production service to
confirm a courtesy disclosure would be rude. Taken on the maintainer's word —
which is why **no rate-limiter code was written**; `fetch_text`'s existing
`429`/`Retry-After` backoff already covers the requirement.

## A pre-existing latent bug found on the way

`fetch_text` wrote `user-agent: DEFAULT_UA` unconditionally and *then* applied
caller headers via `RequestBuilder::header`, which **appends rather than
replaces**. Any caller passing a `user-agent` would have sent **two header
lines**. Nothing did yet, so it had never fired.

Fixed properly with a `FetchOptions::user_agent` override — `None` leaves every
other board on the unchanged `DEFAULT_UA`, which matters because several boards
depend on looking like an ordinary browser. All ~15 `FetchOptions` construction
sites were checked for `..Default::default()` before adding the field.

## Two judgement calls

**`reality=fresh` is unconditional, with no setting.** Every other aggregator
quality lever here (`sort_by=date`, `dedupe_by_url`) is already always-on with no
user-facing knob; a bespoke toggle for one facet on one last-resort tier would be
the odd one out.

**`meta.ignored_params` is treated as an error, not a warning that still returns
data.** It reuses the existing silent-degradation boundary rather than inventing
a signalling path. This is the finding that worried me most: a mistyped filter
returns the whole catalogue and **looks exactly like a legitimate broad result**.
Silently presenting unfiltered results as filtered is the one outcome that is not
acceptable.

## Mutations executed

Five, each broken → run → confirmed red → restored → re-run green:
the `posted_within_days` floor, the identifying UA, the `fetch_text`
replace-not-append fix, the `ignored_params` guard, and `reality=fresh`.

## Out of scope

**`cities` is deliberately not added.** It is real, but geography is a single
**OR-group**: `countries=gb` → 89,211 while `countries=gb&cities=London` →
**89,617**. Adding a city to narrow a country makes results *grow*. That needs a
location-UI decision, not a parameter.

## Provenance note

These two commits were originally authored before today's history rewrite, lost
when I pruned unpushed local branches ahead of it, and recovered from the backup
bundle as patches replayed onto rewritten `main` — so the shas differ from the
originals. Re-verified after replay: 17 freehire tests, 41 http tests, clippy
clean with `-D warnings`.

title: docs: repoint the audit-report sha after the history rewrite
body:
Cleanup after the history rewrite in #1033.

The rewrite renamed every commit, so the `git show <sha>:AUDIT_REPORT.md`
pointer that ADR-0005 and ADR-0006 carry went dead the moment it landed.

Translated through filter-repo's `commit-map`: **`65ea4188c` → `cd1219ef7`**,
verified to still hold all 1,588,368 bytes.

Both citations now also record that the sha **has already moved once** and name
PR #1000 as the durable anchor. A bare sha is exactly the kind of reference a
rewrite breaks; a reader who hits a dead one shouldn't have to guess what to do.

## Known and deliberately not fixed

`CHANGELOG.md` carries a commit link for every release — **all of them now point
at pre-rewrite shas.** That file is generated by semantic-release across 241
tags, so hand-editing it is neither feasible nor durable.

Those links keep resolving today because GitHub doesn't garbage collect on its
own and this repo has forks sharing the object store. They break if that ever
changes. Accepted: the alternative is rewriting generated release history to
chase link cosmetics.

title: feat(scraping): remember which boards actually work between runs
body:
Track B1 of the architecture audit. A board scrape currently forgets everything
the moment it ends: a source that has failed the last nine runs looks exactly
like one that has never been tried. This adds a small per-board reliability
store (`board_health.db`), derives a verdict from it, and surfaces that verdict
on the board chips and the autopilot card.

Five states: `Healthy`, `Failing`, `Flaky`, `Stale`, `Unknown`. `Flaky` is the
one that earns its keep, because it catches the pattern a consecutive-failure
counter structurally cannot see: a board that works often enough to never build
a streak while failing a meaningful share of the runs that reach it.

## What review changed, since that is most of the value here

Two independent architecture passes and a sibling audit, each verified by
executed mutation rather than by reading. Everything below was found, not
designed in.

**Two HIGHs, both closed and both re-proven by mutation:**

- Unbounded renderer-driven row creation. The health store is keyed on board id,
  and the id came from the renderer, so an unrecognised id could mint a row.
  Now filtered on the resolver (not the registry, which fails the fake-resolver
  tests), and the guard asserts `tracked_boards()` — a `COUNT(*)` — because the
  predecessor's `health_for(id).is_none()` shape could not see a row created
  under an id nobody thought of.
- The recovery path left `failing_since` and `last_error` on disk. A
  `COALESCE(board_health.failing_since, excluded.failing_since)` mutation, and
  four variants of it, all die against
  `a_recovery_clears_the_streak_columns_on_disk_not_just_in_memory`.

**Three MEDIUMs, measured rather than argued:**

- **The `Flaky` verdict used lifetime counters**, so it had inertia in both
  directions. A board that had a 10-run outage and then worked *perfectly* kept
  rendering `unreliable · failed 10 of N runs` for **31 flawless runs**; a board
  with 100 clean runs that started failing **every other run** stayed unbadged
  for **100 more**. Now a decayed rolling window: 16 runs and 14 runs/7 failures
  respectively.
- **The positional zip in the engine was correct but untestable.** Replacing it
  with `enumerate()` left the entire suite green, because the guard test put its
  only valid board at index 0. The discriminating shape is a rejected id ahead
  of two *failing* boards, and that test now exists.
- **`neverWorkedSince` rendered "has never worked here · failing for 2 days
  ago"**, because `timeAgo` returns a relative phrase. The existing chips test
  mocks `t()` down to `key:opts` and could never see it, so the new test calls
  the real unmocked `i18n.t`.

**One correctness bug in the fix for the first MEDIUM.** The decay rescales
`failed` proportionally rather than halving it independently, because
independent halving rounds `failed` down less than an odd `verified` and can
*manufacture* a Flaky verdict out of pure rounding (17/4 = 23.5% halves to
8/2 = 25.0%, on a plain success run). But the rescale was done in `u32`:
`failed.saturating_mul(next_verified)` overflows past ~4.29e9 and clamps
**before** the divide, so a board that failed 150,000 of 200,000 runs decayed to
2-in-12, read 16%, and came out Healthy. Fixed in `u64`.

The existing oversized-tally test could not catch that, because it asserts only
that the cap is respected — and the cap *is* respected while the ratio is being
destroyed. The replacement anchors on an absolute floor instead: a board failing
three runs in four must not decay to something better than a coin flip.

## Known and recorded, not fixed

- **`FLAKY_WINDOW_CAP` bounds runs, not time.** At the daily autopilot cadence
  that is one to two weeks, close to `STALE_AFTER_MS`. For someone scraping
  manually several times an afternoon, the same 16 runs span hours and the
  verdict forgets the morning by evening. Documented at the constant.
- **`keys.boards.health` is invalidated on every job event**, which during a
  watched-company scrape means once per company. It rides the invalidation
  cadence `keys.jobs.all` already had, and each one is a small local SQLite
  read, so this is an accepted cost rather than an oversight.
- **`updated_at` is written and never read.** Every question it could answer is
  answered more precisely by `last_success_at`, `last_verified_at` or
  `failing_since`, all of which `derive_status` already reads. It is redundant
  rather than unused; dropping it is a one-line migration and is not done here.

## Not verified

No visual check of the chips or the autopilot card.

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Added cross-run board health indicators showing failing, stale, flaky, healthy, and unknown statuses.
  * Board summaries now display reliability details, failure counts, timing, and sanitized diagnostic tooltips.
  * Added live board-health updates after job activity.
  * Added factory-reset support to clear stored board health history.

* **Privacy**
  * Machine-specific health data is excluded from saved runs and exports.
  * Diagnostic messages now consistently redact sensitive URLs, paths, credentials, hosts, and email addresses.

* **Localization**
  * Added English and German translations for board health statuses.

title: fix(landing): serve the /world clips from r2, which can send cors headers
body:
Fixes the `/world` route, which #1031 broke. It is live and degraded right now:
poster stills render, no video.

## What went wrong, and why the check missed it

`scrub-engine.js` loads each clip with:

```js
fetch(url).then((r) => (r.ok ? r.blob() : ...)).then((blob) => { v.src = URL.createObjectURL(blob); })
```

That is a **cross-origin `fetch`**, so the response must carry
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. **GitHub release downloads do not send it.** Every
clip fetch threw, the engine's fetch-failure path swallowed it, and the route
silently fell back to poster stills.

I verified #1031 with `curl`, which returned `302 → 200`. **`curl` sends no
`Origin` header, so it never exercises CORS at all.** That is the whole reason a
broken change looked verified.

## Why R2 rather than another workaround

The constraint is "the response needs a CORS header". Options:

| | |
|---|---|
| Same-origin (back into `public/`) | Works, but restores the Pages 100 GB/month ceiling — ~5,000 visits at this route's 20 MB device cap |
| Next.js `/api` proxy | **Impossible.** `output: 'export'` means no server; API Routes are a build error and Route Handlers must be `force-static` |
| Build-time fetch into `public/` | Works, but is same-origin again — identical bandwidth exposure |
| **R2 bucket + CORS policy** | Fixes the actual constraint, **and** egress is unmetered so the ceiling is gone rather than moved |

## Configuration applied

- Bucket `aijobhunter-assets`, **Standard** class (Infrequent Access bills separately and does not count toward the free tier)
- 33 objects under `world/vid/`, uploaded with
  `cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` — honest because a new
  clip set means new keys, never mutated ones
- CORS allowlist: the site origin, its `www`, and `localhost:3000` so plain
  `next dev` works with no override
- Custom domain `cdn.aijobhunter.app`, **min TLS raised 1.0 → 1.2**
- **`r2.dev` public URL left disabled** — it bypasses zone cache rules and WAF,
  so it is an unprotected path straight to the bucket

## Verified against the live origin this time

A real `fetch().then(r => r.blob())` executed on the deployed page:

```json
{ "origin": "https://aijobhunter.app", "status": 200,
  "blobBytes": 2503061, "blobType": "video/mp4",
  "ms": 237, "objectUrlOk": true }
```

Plus headers checked directly: the allow-origin header is **present** for this
origin and **absent** for a disallowed one (which still returns 200 — CORS is
enforced by the browser on the header's absence, another way this fails quietly).

## Tests pin the host, not the URL shape

That is where the defect lived: a same-origin `/world/vid/...` path and a GitHub
release URL both look correct and both break the route.

**Mutation-checked by execution against each of those two states in turn — each
turns three tests red.** Neither would have been caught by the previous
assertions.

## Follow-up

The `world-assets-v1` GitHub release stays until this merges and deploys, as a
fallback. It gets deleted after that.

title: chore: drop the 1.5 mb audit report from the tree, keep it in history
body:
Deletes `AUDIT_REPORT.md` (1.5 MB, 4,272 lines) from the working tree and
repoints the two ADRs that cite it.

## Why delete rather than update

It was never a living document. It is a one-off full-history logic audit with a
**fixed scope**: every commit from the initial release through `v0.123.0`
(2026-07-07). Updating it would mean re-running the whole multi-agent audit, and
the result would be a different snapshot, not a newer version of this one.

Six weeks and roughly two hundred commits later, all 141 of its findings carry
`path:line` citations into a HEAD that no longer exists. The most likely way to
use the file today is to be misled by it.

Its top findings are already closed, which is the point:

- `p2-contra-cross-001` (HIGH) — "the privacy guarantee is materially false" is
  now the enumerated third-party disclosure in README/SECURITY, the
  machine-readable inventory in `tests/egress.rs`, and ADR-0005.
- `renderer-feat-3-001` (HIGH) — the orphaned support subtree is gone;
  `features/support/components/` now contains only `SupportPage/`, resolved by
  ADR-0006 to FAQ-only.

61% of the lines were §2 Requirements Ledger and §3 Traceability Matrix, two
machine-generated tables nobody reads twice.

## Nothing is lost

`git show 65ea4188c:AUDIT_REPORT.md` returns all 1,588,368 bytes. Verified. The
two citing ADRs now point there explicitly, with the caveat that the report's
line numbers belong to that commit rather than to HEAD.

## Second commit: a pre-push hook bug this uncovered

The docs/meta fast path piped its changed-file list straight into prettier. That
list is a **diff**, so it includes deletions, and prettier exits non-zero on a
path it cannot open:

```
[error] No files matching the pattern were found: "AUDIT_REPORT.md".
husky - pre-push script failed (code 123)
```

**Every commit that deleted a markdown file was unpushable**, with an error
pointing at the deleted file rather than at the hook. Now filtered to paths that
still exist, with `xargs -r` so a deletions-only commit does not invoke prettier
with zero arguments and silently walk the entire tree.

## One note for the next person

The report itself held **63 of the repo's ADR citations**, so
`check:adr-citations` drops from 913 to 850 against its `MIN_CITATIONS` floor of
800. The floor still holds and the guard is green, but the headroom is now 50
rather than 113. A future bulk deletion is likelier to trip it — and tripping it
would be the guard working, not breaking.

title: fix(resume-pipeline): resolve a fabrication remove by its anchored line
body:
The renderer half of the Major finding CodeRabbit raised on #1024. The Rust half
shipped with that PR; this closes the TS side, which merged into `main` still
wrong.

## The defect

`fabrications.ts` was internally inconsistent about how it identifies an entry.

`removeEvidenceLines` is anchored on `entry.line`, by exact whitespace-trimmed
line equality, and its doc comment says outright **"never by searching for
`evidence`"** — with the reasoning spelled out: a short span matches lines it
was never about, so a substring search deletes the wrong thing.

But `evidencePresent`, which `isFabricationResolved`, `presentFabrication` and
`unresolvedCount` all decide on, did exactly what that doc forbids:

```ts
return !!span && documentText.includes(span);
```

So the app **deleted** by line anchor and **decided resolution** by bare
substring. The user removes the flagged line, the removal succeeds, and if the
span occurs anywhere else in the document the entry never reads resolved — the
integrity chip stays off green and the run stays `needsReview` over work that is
genuinely done. Short spans make that routine: a certification acronym that also
appears in a skills list, or a two-character language code sitting inside
ordinary words.

## The rule

A `remove` verdict now prefers the anchored `line` — resolved once that exact
trimmed line is no longer anywhere in the document — falling back to the
`evidence` substring only when the entry carries no `line`. That absence is a
**supported state**, not a bug: reports persisted before the field existed have
none.

Same field priority as Rust's `entry_resolved`, deliberately, because a
heuristic duplicated across Rust and TS that then drifts is its own recurring
defect class in this repo.

`evidencePresent` is unchanged and still drives the `pending`/`orphaned` split
for undecided entries — that is a rendering question ("can we show the flagged
span"), not a resolution question.

## The alternative, and why it was rejected

The obvious-looking stronger rule is to require **both** signals: the line is
gone AND the evidence is gone. That was mutation-tested rather than argued
about, and it flips the regression test back to red — ANDing reintroduces the
exact bug, because the bare span legitimately survives elsewhere, so
"evidence gone" is false forever and the entry sticks unresolved.

The residual gap is real and worth stating: an entry whose line is **reworded in
place** while still containing the fabricated span reads as resolved. There is
no honest anchor that survives an in-place edit without relocating the line by
searching for the bare span, which is precisely the operation
`removeEvidenceLines` forbids. Rust's shipped fix takes the same cost.

## Verification

Two mutations executed by hand, each watched red then green: reverting
`fabrications.ts` to its pre-fix `main` content (both new regression tests fail),
and the AND variant above.

`tsc --noEmit` clean, ESLint `--max-warnings 0` clean with no disables added,
and 951/951 across `lib/generate`, `components/generation` and `TailorFlow`.

Every caller checked for dependence on the old semantics:
`FabricationReview.tsx`, `QualityBadge.tsx`, `useTailorPipeline.ts`, and
`QualityReportPanel.pipeline.test.tsx` — none of whose fixtures exercised the
"span recurs elsewhere" case, which is why none of them caught this.

title: refactor(landing): serve the /world clips from a release, not from the repo
body:
Moves 33 files / 62 MB of `/world` background video out of the tree and onto the
[`world-assets-v1`](https://github.com/saeedkolivand/ai-job-hunter-app/releases/tag/world-assets-v1)
release. Two separate problems, one move.

## Problem 1: git weight, and specifically the *rate*

Video does not delta-compress, so a re-encode writes every byte again rather
than a diff. One re-encode round had already put **~38 MB of unreclaimable
history** in the pack. The 62 MB level was survivable; the growth rate was not.

## Problem 2: a Pages bandwidth ceiling nobody had noticed

This is the one that actually justifies the change. Sitting in
`apps/landing/public/`, the clips were built into the published Pages site — so
every view drew on GitHub Pages' **100 GB/month soft bandwidth limit**. At this
route's 20 MB device-set cap that is **roughly 5,000 visits a month** before
HTTP 429s.

Release assets are a different pool. From GitHub's docs, verbatim: *"There is no
limit on the total size of a release, nor bandwidth usage."*

To be precise about what changed: GitHub still serves the bytes. They just no
longer count against the metered Pages pool.

## What stays

The **poster stills stay in the repo and on Pages** — ~2 MB total, and they must
paint before any video is fetched. Only the clips move.

## Shape of the change

Every clip URL now goes through a single `vid()` helper pinned to a release
**tag**. Pinning is deliberate: publishing `world-assets-v2` and bumping one line
is atomic, whereas mutating an existing release's assets in place would leave
cached clients disagreeing with fresh ones.

`NEXT_PUBLIC_WORLD_VIDEO_BASE=/world/vid` restores local files for offline work,
and the directory is gitignored so a local copy cannot be re-committed by
accident.

## Tests

The two tests asserting every asset path starts with `/world/` **split in two**,
because that invariant now holds for the posters and not for the clips.

Both halves assert against **literals**, not against the config's own base — so a
regression cannot move the expectation along with the value it is checking. A
fourth test pins every clip to a single tag, so a partial bump cannot ship.

**Mutation-checked by execution:** pointing the base back at `/world/vid` turns
two of them red; restoring turns them green. 34/34.

## Verified

- `next build` clean; the built output contains the release URL and **zero
  remaining `/world/vid/` references**
- published site **~74 MB → 12 MB**
- `tsc --noEmit`, prettier, and `check:landing-drift` all green
- a real `curl` of a release asset returns 302 → 200

## Not verified

`/world` has not been opened in a browser against the release URLs. The build
output and the asset fetch are both checked, but the scroll route itself is not
visually confirmed.

title: docs(persistence): state that the persisted record is authoritative and events only notify
body:
Track C2 of the architecture audit, and the last one. #1013 fixed a symptom,
#1015/#1016 made the question mechanical — this writes down the rule both were
enforcing, which was followed everywhere and stated nowhere. The consequence of
that silence: the deliberate JSON-store exceptions read as accidents.

## The rule, and the half that gets skipped

> The durable record is the truth. An event only says the record changed.

The converse is the load-bearing part: **an event may be missed.** A listener is
registered on mount and torn down on unmount, but the Rust work it describes does
not unmount with it — so everything emitted while the user was elsewhere,
*including the terminal event*, is delivered to nobody, and a React Query
`onSuccess` invalidation belongs to an observer that no longer exists.

Therefore nothing may exist only as an event. A surface that cannot re-derive on
mount is a defect, not a style choice.

The **transient boundary** is framed as one question — "is there work outside
this process that outlives the component?" — with a preference ladder: re-read
the backend record → keep only the *handle* in the app-lifetime session store →
never split a derived value from what it is derived from (that third one is
exactly how #1019's data loss happened).

## Reconcile at open

A persisted record can also be wrong: if the process dies mid-run,
`status = running` outlives the run. The three stores that record in-flight
status disagree about this, and the doc says so with the gaps named —
`jobs.db` sweeps but only within 24 h, `autopilots.json` sweeps unbounded,
`pipeline_runs.db` not at all. The sharp form of the last one (the #1020
lockout) is that `ensure_latest_run` **never reads status**, so no sweep can fix
it on its own.

## Drift found while verifying, and fixed

The existing `DataStore` table was wrong in both directions: it listed
`NotificationStore`, `EmailWatchStore` and `KvCache` as implementations when
none are — which is *why* they sit outside the backup bundle — and omitted
`AutopilotStore`, `DedupStore`, `DiscoveredCompanyStore` and `PipelineRunStore`.
The `KvCache` path did not exist. Line-number citations and the hand-copied
`Resettable` membership list are now pointers, since both were already stale.

The accepted-inconsistencies table also names what the three JSON stores are
inconsistent about *with each other*, not just with SQLite: only
`interactions.json` writes atomically and quarantines a corrupt file;
`notifications.json` reads a corrupt file as empty and then overwrites it, and
is in no backup bundle at all.

## Second commit: a debt note that overstated its debt

`use-resume-pipeline-session.ts` is the entry the guard calls its largest, and
its note claimed the session store keeps the stage but not the run handle, so a
remounted panel "can neither display nor cancel". That stopped being true when
#992 added `applicationApply.applyRun` — verified against the source: `TailorFlow`
hands it back as `initialRunId`/`initialJobId`, the hook re-reads the run record
and replays its persisted stage trail, and `cancelJob` is wired. What is actually
lost is narrower: the streamed draft/letter/thinking text is `useState` with no
durable transcript, so a reconnected run jumps to the finished document.

Corrected, because a debt list that overstates its debt misdirects the next fix.

## Routing left open

`adr-006-generation-session-store.md` is stale — it points at
`renderer/store/generation-store/`, which does not exist, and its stated
mechanism drifted too. A path-only patch would make a still-wrong ADR *look*
current, so it is untouched; it wants an amendment or a superseding record.

## Verification

`pnpm check:agent-system`, `check:adr-citations` (915 citations resolve),
`check:landing-drift`, `check:event-subscriptions` — all green.

title: feat(validate): catch invented tenure, certifications and education
body:
## What

Three new deterministic fabrication checks in `validate::content`, for claims a
model can invent that nothing previously caught: years of experience,
certifications, and degrees the source résumé never mentions.

| Code | Severity | Evidence it rests on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `factual.unsourced_certification` | **Critical** | An uppercase, word-bounded token from a curated 23-entry acronym list |
| `factual.unsourced_credential` | Warning | Unbounded prose in 7 languages, discriminated by adjacency + 3 curated vocabularies |
| `factual.inflated_experience` | Warning | Tenure claims parsed from unbounded prose in 7 languages |

## The part worth reviewing: why one code became two

`factual.unsourced_certification` originally covered two arms resting on very
different evidence, and the code table is what assigns severity — so the weaker
arm inherited the stronger one's Critical.

- The **acronym** arm reads no prose. Each token means one thing on a résumé in
  any language, and four review rounds produced no false positive from it. It
  keeps Critical.
- The **issuer** arm reads natural language. It shipped "4 of 4 fixed,
  measured" and broke on the next pass, then shipped "7 of 7 fixed, measured"
  and broke again. Same evidence class and same cadence as the tenure check,
  so it is now a separate code at Warning.

`factual.inflated_experience` ships as a **Warning** even though the numeric
criterion permitted a Critical (0 false positives across 25 truthful
documents). The argument is the input shape, not the count: two review rounds
each found registers that produced a false Critical, and the corpus was green
before every one of them was named. The cost is also asymmetric — this code
routes to `SectionKey::Summary`, so a false Critical would spend provider calls
rewriting a correct summary and could pressure the model into *understating* a
tenure the candidate really has.

## Defects found and fixed during review, not by the harness

- **The unreadable-tenure guard was an off switch.** It matched any letter-word
  before any year-word anywhere in the source, so one bullet reading "Cut cloud
  spend by 1.2M USD per year" silenced the whole check for that document.
- **The clause-shape rule read sentences about systems as claims about people**,
  15/15 — "Rebuilt a platform with 15 years of accumulated technical debt". The
  measured discriminator is the *subject* position, so the subject must now name
  a person or be absent.
- **A bare acronym under a Certifications heading was invisible.**
  `split_sections` promotes a lone `CISSP` to a heading, so it lived in
  `Section::heading` and no line scan reached it — a hole in the one arm whose
  evidence justifies a Critical. 16 of the 23 curated acronyms were reachable
  that way.
- **Attributive vendor terms are not credentials.** "Docker Certified images",
  "Certified Scrum team" — 7 of 7 fired. A certification names a *role*, so one
  must now appear within a bounded token window.

## Calibration harness

The calibration asserts on the **extracted** column, not only the flagged one.
That gap is why two over-corrections shipped past a green harness: a check that
has been switched off and a check that has been fixed both report zero false
positives. The set of fixtures with non-empty extraction is pinned as a
hand-written membership list, because a set compared against itself cannot
notice a deletion.

14 mutation checks, each re-verified by execution rather than by reading. One
was found unguarded during that re-verification — deleting the adjacency rule
left the suite green — and now has a case that binds it.

## Not verified

No visual/end-to-end check against a real generation run; this is validated at
the unit and calibration level only.

title: feat(match): report hard constraints beside the score instead of blending them into it
body:
Track **E1** of the architecture audit. The honest result is not the one the audit asked for.

## The ask

`combined = 0.6*semantic + 0.4*ats` blends everything, so a candidate failing a non-negotiable still scores on keyword overlap. Add a hard-constraint pass, reported **separately** from the relevance score.

## The finding: this app cannot deliver a knock-out on the data it has

Four constraints were candidates. All four were refused, and each for a specific reason rather than for effort:

| constraint | why not |
| --- | --- |
| **work authorization** (the audit ranked it first) | the app stores **nothing** about it. The only proxy is the candidate's address, and "lives in Germany" is not evidence of lacking US authorization |
| **employment type** | no persisted candidate preference. `AutopilotTarget::work_type` is a per-search filter, and it is a work *arrangement*, not an employment type |
| **salary floor** | `salary_expectation` is free text ("80k DOE") answering an application's salary *question*. No currency, no period, and the posting side is structured on one board only — a verdict needs a money parser plus an FX assumption, two invented facts each time |
| **location** | see below |

Location looked viable and was implemented. Review then established that `job_preferences.location` is a **search-personalization** field — its own translation string reads *"to personalize search results and recommendations"*, and `JobsPage` seeds the scrape form from it one-way with the comment *"Picking a location here never writes back to settings."*

The concrete failure: Settings says `Berlin` from onboarding, the user deliberately searches `Austin` because they are relocating, and every Austin posting returns `notMet`. Executing the real rule found **25 of 38 realistic pairs** returning `notMet` on jobs the candidate could take — `Germany`↔`Berlin`, `San Francisco`↔`Bay Area`, `Vienna`↔`Wien`, `Tokyo`↔`東京`, `Berlin`↔`Telecommute`. Aggravated by **Adzuna never writing `extra.remote`**, so on the primary aggregator remote detection falls entirely to 11 text markers its location strings never carry.

The rule the code states about itself convicts it: a `NotMet` requires positive evidence on **both** sides, and a failed substring match is *absence* of evidence.

**So `NotMet` ships unreachable.** `no_shipped_constraint_can_emit_a_knock_out` pins that it is unreachable, not merely unused, and it remains the contract slot a future constraint will use.

## What does ship, and why it is still worth having

- **The separate channel.** The verdict is computed after `score_one` returns and merged as a sibling field — never a multiplier, never a penalty. This is not hygiene: `score_one`'s result is cached under scoring inputs only, so a verdict frozen into that row would be served stale for the whole TTL the moment the user edited their preferences. Outside the kernel, a cache *hit* still gets a fresh verdict.
- **Four statuses**, not three: `met` / `unknown` / `noPreference` — the last kept distinct because it is the one the user can fix. Each check carries **both sides' own words**, so "positive evidence on both sides" is a checkable property of the payload rather than a promise, enforced in a sealed constructor (`ConstraintCheck` lives in its own module; a struct literal outside it is a compile error).
- **A three-valued matcher.** `location_verdict` splits `Remote` / `PlaceMatch` / `PlaceOverlap` / `Mismatch` / `Undecided`; `location_mismatch` is now exactly the `Mismatch` projection, so the scrape filter is unchanged. Proven by a **1,968-pair differential** across empties, umlaut/transliteration triples, exonyms, non-Latin, multi-location and country-code-only specs: **0 diffs**.

The principle, recorded in the module: **reuse the matcher, re-derive the epistemics.** The identical predicate is safe as a scrape filter — one location typed seconds ago, one row, reversible — and unsafe as a published verdict against every cached posting keyed off a settings field.

## A trade-off you should see, not discover

`met` now requires a **whole-token** match, so `San Francisco` no longer reads `met` against `San Diego` on the shared `san` token. The cost: a request *more specific* than the posting — `Berlin, Germany` against a bare `Berlin` — now reads `unknown` rather than `met`.

The UI's default preference values are `'San Francisco, CA'`, `'Berlin, Germany'`, `'New York, NY'`, so **this is not a rare path**. It loses a true positive and never states a false one, and `unknown` claims nothing. Reversible in one match arm if you disagree.

Implementation note: exonyms must expand **per token**, not over the whole needle list — expansion adds a word the user never wrote, so a naive "every needle must match" rule would fail the exact `Munich`/`München` pair the curated table exists to bridge.

## Verification

**19 mutation checks, all caught**, including three that survived earlier rounds: an `include_str!` wiring pin blind to `let _ = attach(…)` and to a commented-out call, and a struct-literal bypass that must now fail to *compile*.

The old `assert_eq!(knock_outs, 4)` was this repo's recurring defect — a corpus containing only pairings the code already agreed with. Replaced with the full hand-derived status distribution over **176 cells**: 44 `noPreference`, 75 `met`, 57 `unknown`, **0 `notMet`**. That last figure as an asserted absolute is what makes the ship claim checkable, and each later tightening had to add the pairing it existed for or the distribution would not have moved.

## Incidental find worth recording

An early `include_str!` assertion embedded a closing brace in a string literal. `tests/egress.rs` strips `#[cfg(test)]` regions with a brace counter that cannot see into string literals, so the literal truncated the stripped region — leaving real code **un-stripped**, which that guard's own message calls "the dangerous direction". The assertion was rewritten to contain no brace rather than adding the file to `KNOWN_EXCEPTIONS`. That guard earned its keep on a change with nothing to do with egress.

## Not built

No renderer surface. The field rides the payload and is in the shared contract with an `isKnockOut` predicate shipped **before** any UI, so a consumer cannot write `status !== 'met'` and silently turn both undecided states into a knock-out.

title: ci: enforce that every adr citation resolves to a real record
body:
Track **F1** of the architecture audit — but not the track as written.

## The stated deliverable was already done

The audit said to merge two ADR trees with colliding numbers. **`docs/adr/` does not exist on `main`** — PR #1000 folded it into `docs/knowledge/decision-records/` two days ago. Checking that before moving anything is the only reason this didn't become a day of re-doing shipped work.

## The real defect was underneath

57 ADRs now live in one directory as two filename series, and **they are disambiguated only by zero-padding**:

- `NNNN-*.md` — the closed ex-`docs/adr/` series, cited `ADR-0001`…`ADR-0023`
- `adr-NNN-*.md` — the open series, cited `ADR-001`…`ADR-034`

**Every number 1–23 collides.** `ADR-010` is untrusted-input fencing; `ADR-0010` is the bridge HMAC handshake. Both live, both correct, distinguished by one character.

That rule was load-bearing and **written down nowhere** — and it had already failed twice in shipped work:

| where | claimed | actual |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0020-crash-reporting.md` | `ADR 0027` | the closed series has no 0027 — mis-padded |
| `docs/ARCHITECTURE_STATUS.md` | `ADR-0025` | ADR-025 is the agent fleet, written three weeks *later*, about something else |

The second is worth dwelling on: re-padding it would have been **worse** than leaving it, because no ADR covers emitter/resource ports at all. It now points at the `TODO(arch)` in `tests/architecture.rs` — the thing that actually tracks it.

## What ships

The rule is documented in `docs/knowledge/README.md` **and enforced**. `pnpm check:adr-citations` verifies every `decision-records/*.md` path reference resolves, every `ADR-NNN` citation resolves under the padding rule, and no citation is 1–2 digits (ambiguous between the series). The ADR inventory is **discovered** from the directory, so a new ADR is covered the day it is written.

```
check:adr-citations OK — 57 ADRs (23 closed `NNNN-`, 34 open `adr-NNN`);
911 number citations (768 hyphen, 143 spaced) and 143 path references
across 2285 tracked files all resolve, none ambiguous.
```

Also closes a guard gap: `checkAdrIndex()` filtered `/^adr-\d+/`, so all 23 closed-series ADRs were invisible to it **in both directions** — dropping an index row or linking a non-existent file both exited 0. Now caught.

## Vacuity floors, per form

Every check here is "this list is empty", which passes trivially against an empty scan. The floors are **per citation form**, not a single total, and that distinction was earned the hard way:

I first specified a single total floor of 700 using a worked example I hadn't measured — "a regex dropping every spaced citation could halve the count". It can't: the spaced form is 143 of 911, ~16%. A total floor can only ever see a form's disappearance *diluted by every other form surviving*, and 800 would merely happen to exceed `911 − 143` today — ~35 new hyphen-cited ADRs restore the total and the hole reopens with no diff anywhere.

So: hyphen ≥ 600, spaced ≥ 100, total ≥ 800 as a backstop. Counts are captured in the **same pass** that resolves the number, so the floors and the resolver cannot guard different populations.

| mutation | result |
| --- | --- |
| spaced form dropped | **exit 1** — `spaced form: 0 found, floor 100` |
| hyphen form dropped | **exit 1** — `hyphen form: 0 found, floor 600` |
| whole pattern dead | **exit 1** — all three floors reported together |
| ADR directory moved | **exit 1** — `Only 0 ADRs found` |
| file walk emptied | **exit 1** — `Only 0 files scanned` |

Both form-loss cases are in the test file, each asserting the *other* form's floor is **not** implicated — so a future change collapsing the two counts into one fails the test rather than quietly passing.

## The guard caught itself

The first version's header comment quoted the two defects verbatim as `ADR 0027` and `ADR-0025`. The file was untracked, so `git ls-files` skipped it and the check passed; staging it flipped it to exit 1 **on its own doc comment**. The examples were reworded rather than adding the script to the exclusion list — an exemption for the file that defines the rule is exactly how a guard becomes decorative. Only two exclusions exist: generated landing snapshots (frozen historical text) and the test file (fixtures are deliberately broken), both commented with why.

32 tests in the new file, 159 across the scripts project.

## What was deliberately not done

**No redirect stubs at `docs/adr/*`.** The brief mandated them; recreating that directory reverses a reviewed decision from two days ago and reopens the invitation to file ADR #24 in the wrong place — the README records that it *"carried no index and no owner, and grew to 23 records because nothing stopped it."* Deep links there have been dead since #1000 either way.

`AUDIT_REPORT.md`'s ADR-0001 / adr-007 contradiction is untouched. That is an architecture decision, not a docs merge.

title: test(pipeline): pin what a killed resume run leaves on disk and what nothing cleans up
body:
Track **C3** of the architecture audit. It was scoped as "one process-kill resume test" — the test exists, but tracing the recovery contract first turned up a **real user-facing defect**, so this PR documents a gap rather than pinning correct behaviour.

## The gap

A résumé pipeline run writes a `pipeline_runs` row with `status = 'running'` **before stage one**, deliberately, so a crash leaves visible evidence. Nothing ever reconciles it:

- `JobTracker::open` sweeps `jobs.db` → `failed` with "Interrupted by app restart" ✅
- `AutopilotStore::mark_interrupted_runs` handles autopilot ✅
- `PipelineRunStore::open` runs migrations and a URL normalizer, **and nothing else** ❌

### It is not just a stale chip

`runs_for_job` orders by `started_at DESC`, so the crashed run is the newest run for that posting **forever**. `ensure_latest_run` therefore makes `resume_pipeline_regenerate_section` and `resume_pipeline_resolve_fabrication` refuse every write against the older run that actually holds the saved document — with the message:

> There is a newer run for this posting… If that run is still going, wait for it to finish.

The user is told to wait for a run that will never finish. **The review tools are locked out for that posting permanently.** The only escapes are paying for another full run, or waiting for three more runs to evict the orphan by retention.

### And a naive fix does not close it

Adding `UPDATE pipeline_runs SET status='failed' WHERE status='running'` at open makes the chip honest — and `newest.id` is *still* the killed run, because `ensure_latest_run` keys on **recency, not status**. Measured, not assumed.

There is also no way to join the two stores today: `RunRow` has no job id, `job_start` records a null payload, and the two ids are generated independently. So `jobs.db` correctly knows a `resumePipeline.run` was interrupted and **nothing on disk links that knowledge to the run row**. Any fix needs a new column/index, or a sweep deciding on the run store's own evidence (a trailing `start` event with no `finish`).

**Nothing here is implemented.** That is a design decision, and it is not a test's to make.

## What the test actually does

**Real: the kill.** The test binary re-executes itself (ignored + env-gated so it can never park a normal suite), the child opens the real `PipelineRunStore` and `JobTracker` on a shared temp dir, and the parent `Child::kill()`s it — `TerminateProcess`, no unwinding, no destructors, no SQLite close. The parent then opens those files having never touched them: genuine process death, committed WAL read back by a fresh process.

**Simulated: the run.** The child writes the run/event/job rows directly rather than executing eight AI stages, which would need a provider, an `AppHandle` and minutes of wall clock. So this proves what happens to *that on-disk state* across a kill; it does not prove the pipeline writes exactly that state. The doc comment says so in those words, and `stage_fixture_matches_the_real_pipeline` pins the fixture's stage names against the real `QUALITY_STAGES` so a rename fails loudly instead of quietly making the fixture fictional.

**Anchoring.** The load-bearing absolute is the `jobs.db` arm: `status == Failed` and `error == Some("Interrupted by app restart")` — values the child never wrote (it wrote `Running` / `None`), so that arm cannot pass by round-tripping.

**No sleeps or races.** The parent blocks on the child's ready line; the child parks on a stdin read the parent holds open. One `Duration` in the file, a 60 s watchdog on a path that completes in ~10 ms.

## Mutation results

| Mutation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Delete the `jobs.db` interrupted sweep | **red** — `left: Running, right: Failed` |
| **Add** pipeline-run reconciliation at open | **red** — `left: "failed", right: "running"` |
| Break the child readiness handshake | **red** at the watchdog (it initially *hung*; fixed with a reader thread + watchdog before shipping) |
| `ensure_latest_run` → `Ok(())` unconditionally | **red** on the lockout assertion |

The second matters most: the gap assertions fail the moment reconciliation is added, so they observe its absence rather than passing vacuously. **These tests are designed to go red when the gap is fixed** — both doc comments say to read such a failure as "the gap was closed, update this test", not as a regression.

## One more thing found, not touched

`JobTracker::open`'s sweep is bounded by `created_at > now − 24 h`. A job older than that keeps `status = 'running'` on disk permanently — invisible, because the same cutoff excludes it from the load. Harmless today, but "the jobs sweep handles it" is only true within 24 hours.

## RUSTSEC-2026-0258

> The h2 crate, used internally by hyper, had a flaw that would accept and queue empty DATA frames without limit. If streams were not actively drained, this could lead to unbounded memory usage, or a panic if the length overflows.

Low severity. We reach it transitively through **both** `hyper 1.10.1` and `reqwest 0.13.4`, not directly.

Lockfile only. `0.4.15` → `0.4.16` is the patched release the advisory names, and `cargo update -p h2` locks it with 173 other dependencies unchanged.

cargo deny check advisories
  before: advisories FAILED
  after:  advisories ok

title: fix(jobs): keep the scrape state alive across a route change
body:
The worst instance of the defect class #1015 now guards: state describing long-running Rust work kept in a route-scoped React component. Three defects, one of them **data loss**.

## 1. "Show more" after a route change wiped the persisted posting list

`startScrape` compares the current search signature against the last one; a difference latches `replace: true`, which makes the backend **clear the postings cache** the instant the first new item streams.

Both halves of that comparison were per-mount. Run a search → go to Settings → come back → press **Show more**, and the entire result set is destroyed by a button whose whole contract is *append*.

My original trace said the search signature alone was at fault. **That was wrong, and the fix is bigger:** `scrapeForm` was also `useState` in `JobsPage`, so a route change reset the *criteria* too. Even with the signature restored, the form reads back as `{boards:[aggregator], query:'', amount:25}` and the comparison legitimately says "different search" → same wipe. Mutation **B** below is that proof: signature stored, form left local, and the end-to-end test is still red. The signature is *derived* from the form, and two derived-from lifetimes that differ desync — the same argument that forced the replace latch to move with it.

"Show more" renders unconditionally whenever there are rows, so the repro needs nothing unusual.

## 2. The in-flight scrape became an uncancellable orphan

`scrapeJobId` died with the component. On remount the command bar showed no progress and no Cancel — while the always-mounted status bar still showed it running — and `startScrape`'s "cancel the previous scrape first" step read a now-null id, so **the next search did not cancel the orphan either**: two scrapes writing into one postings cache.

## 3. Per-board diagnostics were lost

`scrapeOutcome` and the summaries hold the "aggregator: 429 rate limited" strip — the one thing that explains an empty result.

**Storing them was not sufficient**, and this is the second thing the trace missed: `useJobEvents` is page-scoped, so `job.completed` is emitted to nobody while unmounted. The job tracker keeps the identical payload, so the watchdog now recovers `result.boards` under `finishScrape`'s existing jobId guard. Five lines, and it's what actually closes defect 3.

## What moved, and what deliberately did not

**Into `JobsSlice`** (which already holds `listScrollTop`, documented as "restored on remount"): the search signature, the replace latch, `scrapeJobId`, the scrape outcome, the summaries, the failure note, and `scrapeForm`.

**Left local, on purpose:** `livePostings` (transient buffer — the backend cache plus the existing throttled invalidation rehydrates it), `pendingFinishRef` (cannot outlive the call that needs it), and **`scraping`**, which stays `useState` seeded from the stored job id. The watchdog remains the reconciler: it keys on `scrapeJobId`, polls the authoritative terminal state, and now settles a remount-onto-a-finished-job on the first tick — tested explicitly, rather than "eventually".

## Mutation checks

Each deletes the *feature*, not a constant:

| | mutation | red tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | signature back to a per-mount ref | 2 |
| B | `scrapeForm` back to `useState` | 1 (the end-to-end one) |
| C | `scrapeJobId` back to `useState` | 10 |
| D | summaries/failure note back to `useState` | 3 |
| E | drop only the watchdog boards recovery | 2 |
| F | `patchScrapeForm` spreads the captured form | 1 |
| G | drop the `job.stream` identity guard | 1 |

The "Show more" test asserts the **wire payload** — `replace === undefined` on the second call, with `replace === true` on the first as an absolute baseline, so a regression that deleted `replace` everywhere cannot pass. Three existing assertions that poked at an internal boolean were replaced with wire-payload assertions for the same reason.

## Test-quality notes

Three sibling `JobsPage` tests mocked the session store with a plain object, which cannot model `getState()` or propagate `setJobs`; they now use the real store seeded per test, and two spy assertions became state assertions. `session-store.test.ts` compared the whole slice to a literal; it now spreads the defaults **plus** six absolute assertions, so a default silently flipping cannot ride along.

## Note

Identity checks inside the event handler read `useSessionStore.getState()` synchronously — the handler runs on backend events, not on React's schedule, so a subscription-captured value would reintroduce exactly the staleness the old ref existed to prevent. The `isActiveJob`-before-`noteScrapeFinished` ordering is unchanged.

title: fix(autopilot): jitter scheduled runs so default installs stop herding
body:
Track **B3** of the architecture audit.

## Why this one is not theoretical

Schedules are clock-anchored, the tick is 60 s wide, and every record created before the run-time picker defaults to **09:00**. So every default-schedule install in a time zone hits the same third-party APIs inside the same minute.

The desktop log already shows scheduled runs failing this way:

```
[autopilot] board 'aggregator' failed (error='adzuna: HTTP 503; ...')
```

## The design decision that matters

**The offset is deterministic per autopilot, derived from its id — not random.**

A random delay would have meant sleeping inside the tick, and that breaks the two properties everything else in this scheduler is built on: catch-up after a missed occurrence, and no-double-run once `lastRunAt` is stamped at or after the occurrence. Both come from the occurrence being a *single well-defined instant*.

Shifting the **occurrence** instead of delaying the **run** keeps that instant well-defined. Catch-up and no-double-run still hold unchanged, and the tests stay reproducible.

Two smaller calls:

- **FNV-1a, not `DefaultHasher`** — the standard hasher is explicitly not guaranteed stable across Rust releases, and an offset that moved on a toolchain bump would silently shift every user's schedule. Ids are UUIDs, so the low bits are already well distributed.
- **Ten minutes** — wide enough to spread a herd across ten tick windows, far enough under the shortest interval (hourly) that a shifted occurrence can never overtake the next one, and small enough that someone who picked 09:00 isn't surprised by what they see.

That upper bound is a `const _: () = assert!(...)` beside the constant rather than a test. A test comparing two constants is a tautology (clippy rejects it, correctly), and this makes a bad value **unbuildable** rather than merely reported.

## Tests

Beyond the offset being stable and in range:

- **the occurrence moves by exactly the offset** — not "roughly", not "is later";
- **the behaviour a user would notice**: between the nominal time and the offset, today's occurrence has *not* been reached, so the most recent one is still yesterday's. A careless implementation gets this backwards and fires early;
- **a full-day, minute-by-minute sweep** asserting exactly one transition — one run per day, no double-run, no skipped day. This is the property the whole feature must not break.

Every pre-existing occurrence test now passes an explicit zero offset rather than inheriting a default, so they still describe the pure clock arithmetic.

## Mutation-checked

Making the offset always zero fails `jitter_actually_spreads_a_herd`:

```
200 autopilots landed in only 1 distinct minutes — the herd is not spread
```

Without that assertion the whole change could be an elaborate no-op and every other test would still pass.

## One thing to note

During verification a single test failed once in a full `cargo test --all-features --locked` run and did not reproduce across two subsequent full runs (4218 passing). The scheduler's `is_due` tests read the live clock, so a minute-boundary flake is the plausible explanation — but I could not reproduce it, so I am flagging it rather than claiming it didn't happen.

title: fix(scripts): stop a doc comment from promoting a hook to a subscriber
body:
Follow-up to #1015. The AI review posted a **HIGH** after the last push and the check went red; #1015 was merged before it was addressed, so this fixes it on `main`.

## The finding was right, and the cause is worse than a stale entry

It reported `features/monitoring/components/MonitoringPage/index.tsx` as declared-but-not-subscribing. Verified: that file imports `useJobQueue`, which is a plain `useQuery` hook with no subscription anywhere in it.

So why did discovery think it was one? Because a declaration slice runs to the *next* `export`, which means **the doc comment belonging to the hook below lands inside the preceding hook's body**. And `use-jobs.ts` documents `useJob` like this:

```
 * HARD REQUIREMENT: a `useJobEvents()` subscription MUST be mounted somewhere in
 * the tree, or this query never updates.
```

That sentence sits in `useJobQueue`'s slice. The transitive closure I added in #1015 saw `useJobEvents(` in the body, promoted the query hook to a subscription hook, and dragged every file calling it into the inventory. **Prose about a hook counted as a call to it.**

This is the same structural fact already recorded in this repo from the other direction — a doc comment sits *above* its item, so anything anchored on the item *before* swallows it.

## The fix

Blank comments and string/template literals before matching. A hook name inside a string is a mention, not a call; a commented-out subscription is not one either.

It is a **scanner, not a regex**, deliberately: `//.*$` would eat the rest of a line after a URL inside a string literal, silently **dropping a real call**. For a guard, a false negative is the one failure direction that cannot be tolerated — it reports green. Characters are replaced one-for-one with spaces so every `match.index` still points at the right place.

## Result

`useJobQueue` correctly drops out — **15 hooks, not 16** — and with it the `MonitoringPage` entry, which is removed.

The other four wrappers were checked by hand and are genuine, so the closure itself was sound:

| hook | why it counts |
| --- | --- |
| `useWorkerActivity` | calls `useJobEvents()` |
| `useAutoIndex` | calls `useJobEvents()` |
| `useMenuIntents` | registers `api.menu.onNavigate` / `onAction` |
| `useUpdater` | subscribes directly |

## Tests

35, up from 29. The new ones pin the shipped bug (the next hook's doc comment), a commented-out call, a listener appearing only inside a string, and that stripping preserves length and line structure so offsets stay valid.

title: test(renderer): make surviving navigation a build-time question, not an audit
body:
## Why

The autopilot bug you reported (#1013) was one instance of a class, not a one-off. A subscription only receives events while its component is mounted — but the Rust work it describes does **not** unmount. Leave the route and three things break at once:

- every event emitted while you were away is dropped, **including the terminal one**, so nothing tells the UI the work ended;
- the component's local progress state was discarded, so it re-renders as idle for work still running;
- a React Query mutation's `onSuccess` invalidation belongs to the unmounted observer, so the result never reaches the cache either.

An audit of the whole renderer found the same shape in the jobs scrape, the résumé pipeline, the Ollama model pull, the embeddings re-index and more. **Auditing again after every new feature is not a plan.** This asks the question at the moment the code is written instead.

## What it does

`pnpm check:event-subscriptions` **discovers** the subscription-hook family from `services/` by the one idiom they all share — `api.<ns>.on<Event>(` — and then requires every file outside `services/` that calls one to be declared with its mount lifetime:

- `always` needs no argument;
- `route-scoped` needs a note saying **what is dropped** and why that is acceptable.

Discovery matters more than the list: a brand-new subscription hook is covered the day it is written, which a hardcoded list could never promise. Both directions are checked, so the inventory cannot rot — an undeclared subscriber fails, and so does a declared file that no longer subscribes.

It is **not** "no route-scoped subscriptions". Some are legitimate; exactly one entry is an accepted non-defect (the monitoring activity feed is a view of the current moment and has no per-run state to preserve), and it says so in its note.

## It earned its keep before it was even wired up

It found **three subscribers the 34-agent audit of this exact question had missed** — all three reaching `useUpdater`, which turns out to have **three independent instances**, each with its own subscription and its own local status. Two are always-mounted (the banner, the menu), so the update itself is never lost; the Settings copy resets to idle on every route change.

## The `route-scoped` entries are a debt list, not approvals

Each one records what that file loses today. The largest, which is worse than the bug that started this:

> `hooks/use-resume-pipeline-session.ts` mounts **four** subscriptions (job events, notifications, pipeline stages, draft stream) and is called from `TailorFlow/GeneratingPanel.tsx` — route-scoped **and** conditionally rendered. A résumé generation runs for minutes; leaving the tab drops its stage events and its streamed draft. The session store keeps the stage but not the run handle, so the remounted panel shows "generating" and can neither display nor cancel it.

Recorded rather than fixed here so each fix is a separate, reviewable change per feature — and so the list cannot silently grow in the meantime.

## Mutation-checked, including the failure mode that would make this theatre

- A new feature file that subscribes → fails **by name**.
- Breaking the discovery regex → trips the **vacuity guards** rather than silently passing everything. Every check here is a set comparison, and a set comparison against an empty discovery passes while checking nothing.

16 unit tests cover the logic against a synthetic tree, plus **three that run against the real renderer**, so discovery drifting off the actual source cannot stay green.

## Placement

`scripts/` beside the other drift guards, not a vitest file: the renderer tsconfig carries no node types, and the `lint-format` CI job has **no path filter**, so a diff that happens to miss the renderer cannot skip this.

## Deliberately not shipped

A companion "state machines must be re-armable" guard. The autopilot machine's real defect was dropping an **unsolicited** backend event in a terminal state, and every predicate I could write for that was either vacuous — all three machines already reach a busy state via `RESET` — or arbitrary. A guard I cannot make bite is worse than none.

title: test(extension): pin the mv3 permission surface against the readme's promises
body:
Track **D2** of the architecture audit — and the last open piece of Track D (D1 shipped as the egress inventory).

## Why

`manifest.ts` is the source of truth for claims this project makes **outside this repo**: to Chrome Web Store and AMO reviewers, in the extension README's "Permissions — minimal & justified" table, and on the landing privacy page.

Nothing asserted any of it. Widening a permission is a two-line edit, and the widened build would reach store review — and the user — with the old justification still printed beside it.

Store review is also the wrong place to find out. A rejection costs a release cycle; an **accepted** over-broad permission costs the claim itself.

## What is pinned, and why in this shape

- **The permission list, written out by hand.** A test that loops over the thing it guards catches additions only — delete an entry and the assertion deletes itself. The literal is the half that notices a *removal*.
- **A denylist** of permissions the extension must never hold. This is the half that survives a careless update, and it's the one that matters most.
- **Host permissions checked as a property**, not by string equality: every entry must *parse* to loopback.
- **Both targets compared to each other**, so a per-target delta cannot smuggle a permission into one build.
- **MV3, no CSP loosening, no static `content_scripts`** — Scan mode injects on a click bounded by `activeTab`; a static block would run unbidden on every matching page, which is a different product.
- **Firefox's `data_collection_permissions: ['none']`** — the assertion to AMO that nothing leaves the device. If that ever stops being true, this test failing is the intended prompt to declare the real categories rather than ship a false one.

## Mutation-checked

| mutation | result |
| --- | --- |
| add `tabs` to the manifest **and to the allowed literal** — the careless-update case | ✅ denylist fails it anyway, both targets |
| swap a host for `http://127.0.0.1.evil.com/*` — a different origin that merely *starts* the same way | ✅ 5 tests fail, including the loopback property |

The second is exactly why the host check parses instead of comparing strings.

## README parity, both directions

The table is the justification a store reviewer and a user actually read, so:

- a permission present in the build and absent from the table is an **undocumented capability**;
- deleting the "we do **not** request `<all_urls>`, `tabs`, `webRequest`" paragraph now fails too — otherwise the denylist would still be enforced while corresponding to nothing published, and the next reader would have no way to know the guard was protecting a promise.

## No new tooling

Test files are excluded from the extension tsconfig, and `rewrite-preset-parity.test.ts` already reads with `node:fs`, so the README check rides an existing precedent.

title: fix(scraping): register jobicy in the shared board list and make the drift impossible
body:
## A board the app offers but the shared contract has never heard of

`SCRAPERS` (`scraping/boards/mod.rs`) holds **24** boards. The renderer's `BOARD_IDS` (`packages/shared/src/schemas/index.ts`) held **23**.

The missing one is **`jobicy`** — and it is not a stub. It is a fully registered scraper with `id() == "jobicy"`, a live-verified HTTP implementation, `listed()` defaulting to `true` so the catalog offers it, and `boards.jobicy` labels already written in **both** `en` and `de`. Everything except the shared list knew about it.

For contrast, the one board that is *deliberately* absent from the picker is `comeet` — it overrides `listed()` to `false`, which is why `engine/test.rs` asserts "23 of the 24 registered boards are listed". And `comeet` **is** in `BOARD_IDS`. So the omission is not a policy, it is an oversight, and neither list could see it because nothing compared them.

## Why it has not bitten yet — and why that is not reassuring

The `z.enum(BOARD_IDS)` looks like it constrains the wire. It does not: `pnpm gen:ipc` lowers enums to strings, so the generated Rust is

```rust
pub struct ScrapeBoardsRequest {
    pub boards: Vec<String>,
    ...
```

and the id that actually crosses IPC is validated by the registry lookup (`boards::get`), which knows `jobicy` perfectly well. The schema's own comment claimed the opposite — that each entry *"is already constrained to a known `BoardId`"* server-side — which is precisely why the gap read as safe to anyone checking. That comment is corrected here rather than left to mislead the next reader.

What is genuinely broken today is the **`BoardId` type**: the renderer programs against a union that omits a board the backend ships. The day anything parses `ScrapeBoardsRequestSchema` at runtime — its stated purpose — `jobicy` breaks.

## The fix

`pnpm gen:ipc` now emits the shared list to `ipc_contracts/board_ids.rs`, exactly the shape as the existing `DATE_FILTER_OPTIONS` / `AI_GENERATE_INTENTS` emitters, so this rides the `gen:ipc:check` CI gate that already exists. A Rust test then compares it against `SCRAPERS` **in both directions**:

- one catches a board added to the registry and forgotten in TS — the `jobicy` case;
- the other catches a board removed from the registry while the TS list still promises it to `BoardId`.

Plus a vacuity guard, because both assertions are "this difference is empty", which is trivially true of two empty lists.

## Mutation-checked

Removing `jobicy` from the shared list again and regenerating:

```
registered here but absent from packages/shared BOARD_IDS: ["jobicy"]
  — add them there and run `pnpm gen:ipc`
the two lists must have the same length, not merely overlap
```

## One thing deliberately NOT done

The audit item that prompted this also asked to derive `assert_eq!(health.scrapers.len(), 24)` from `SCRAPERS.len()`. I left the literal alone: driving that assertion off the very list it guards makes it **vacuous** — it is the only check that notices a scraper being deleted, and `SCRAPERS.len() == SCRAPERS.len()` notices nothing. The parity test removes the duplication that actually drifts; the literal keeps guarding the thing a self-referential count cannot.
